rationale: Both oracles report a message from the Lord sent among the nations, calling them to rise for war against Idumea. The shared summons and named nation connect the two announcements.
Obadiah announces that Idumea has been made insignificant and dishonored among the nations. Jeremiah likewise describes her as made small among nations and despised among people.

Both Idumea oracles connect the heart's pride or insolence with holes in rocks and an elevated position. Obadiah voices the inhabitant's boast as a question about who can bring him down. Jeremiah announces that the Lord will bring the addressee down despite the elevated eagle's nest.

Obadiah describes soaring like an eagle and placing a nest among the stars, then announces that the Lord will bring the addressee down from there. Jeremiah likewise joins the elevated eagle's nest with the Lord bringing the addressee down.

Both passages compare Idumea's loss with grape gatherers and thieves at night. Obadiah asks whether ordinary gatherers would leave a gleaning; Jeremiah announces gatherers who leave no remnants, sharpening the devastation described by the shared imagery.

Obadiah describes Esau searched out and his hidden things seized. Jeremiah likewise names Esau, then says their secrets are uncovered and they cannot hide, preserving that passage's change to plural pronouns.

Obadiah's covenant partners and men at peace become opponents and set ambushes. The psalm similarly laments treachery from a trusted man of peace, presenting the reversal of an expected peaceful relationship.

relationship: parallel loss of the wise and their counsel
rationale: Obadiah announces destruction of the wise out of Idumea and understanding out of Mount Esau. Jeremiah's Idumea oracle addresses the loss of wisdom in Teman and counsel among the discerning.

Obadiah describes Teman's warriors terrified so that a person may be removed from Mount Esau. Jeremiah joins judgment concerning Teman with Idumea's strong men's hearts becoming like the heart of a woman in labor.

Obadiah condemns violence and impiety toward the brother Jacob. Deuteronomy explicitly forbids abhorring an Edomite because he is a brother, making the kinship obligation relevant to the violence condemned here.

relationship: parallel judgment for violence against Judah
rationale: Obadiah gives slaughter and impiety toward Jacob as the reason for Esau's shame and removal. Ezekiel similarly grounds judgment on Idumea in its vengeance and grudge against Judah's house.
Obadiah condemns the slaughter of Jacob by his brother. Joel specifically announces Idumea's desolation because of injustice toward Judah's sons and the shedding of righteous blood.

Obadiah places Esau alongside foreigners who enter Jerusalem's gates and take its strength. The psalm remembers Edom's sons urging Jerusalem's destruction down to its foundations, likewise treating them as participants in her calamity.

relationship: parallel accusation of dispossession and lots
rationale: Obadiah describes foreigners taking strength captive and casting lots over Jerusalem. Joel presents the Lord judging the nations over scattered Israel, the division of His land and lots cast over His people.

relationship: shared prohibition of rejoicing at another's fall
rationale: Obadiah forbids rejoicing and boasting over Judah's destruction and affliction. Proverbs likewise forbids rejoicing when even an enemy falls, explaining that such delight displeases the Lord.

relationship: parallel condemnation of exploiting Israel's ruin
rationale: Obadiah forbids entering the afflicted people's gates and joining attacks on their strength. Ezekiel condemns Mount Seir for claiming the two countries and treating Israel's desolate mountains as food, describing another form of exploitation of Israel's calamity.

Obadiah forbids blocking escape routes to destroy or confine fugitives. Ezekiel accuses Mount Seir of treacherously ambushing Israel's house with the sword; both condemn violence directed at Israel in its distress.

relationship: parallel repayment upon the aggressor's head
rationale: Obadiah announces that a nation's own actions will be repaid upon its head. Joel uses that same repayment language when condemning the seizure of treasures and the sale of Judah's people.

Obadiah moves from drinking on the holy mountain to the nations drinking and going down. In the Jeremiah account, the nations receive the Lord's wine cup of judgment, with Jerusalem and Judah heading the listed recipients. Obadiah locates salvation on Mount Zion. Joel likewise locates escape on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem within the promise that those calling on the Lord's name will be saved.

relationship: Israel as the agent of judgment on Idumea
rationale: Obadiah pictures Jacob and Joseph as fire consuming Esau's stubble. Ezekiel states that the Lord will place His vengeance on Idumea by the hand of His people Israel; both place Israel in the role of executing that judgment.

relationship: parallel inheritance of Edom by Jacob
rationale: Obadiah includes possession of Esau's mountain in Israel's future holdings. Balaam's oracle likewise calls Edom and Esau an inheritance and speaks of one arising from Jacob.

Obadiah promises possession of Esau's mountain and further territories. Ezekiel records Mount Seir's claim to possess the two countries and Israel's desolate mountains; the passages present opposing claims and a reversal of who will possess the land.

Obadiah links Jerusalem's deportation with future inheritance of cities in the Negeb. Jeremiah promises renewed acquisition of fields, explicitly including the Negeb's cities, because the Lord will bring back the exiles. The connection concerns restored possession rather than identifying Obadiah's Ephrathah with another place.

relationship: parallel judgment on Esau through God's people
rationale: Obadiah describes saved men ascending from Zion to execute judgment on Esau's mountain. Ezekiel similarly says the Lord's vengeance on Idumea will be carried out by His people Israel.

relationship: shared kingship of the Lord over the nations
rationale: Obadiah concludes that the kingdom will belong to the Lord after judgment on Esau. The psalm declares that kingship belongs to the Lord and that He rules the nations, setting the individual oracle within that wider sovereignty.
